blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Missing data are values that were intended to be recorded but were not. Values that do not apply (a question skipped by design) are structurally missing and are not missing data in this sense.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Every method so far assumed a complete dataset. Real data lose values: skipped questions, missed visits, lost samples. Whether the losses bias the answer depends on why values are missing (§15.4.1), and that decides the handling (§15.4.2–15.4.3).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In data/cbhi_survey.csv, sought_formal_care is blank for the 351 households without a sick child, reason_not_joining is blank for the 150 members, and satisfaction_1to5 is blank for the 350 non-members. All three are structurally missing: the question did not apply. A household that refused to state its income would be genuinely missing. In the §12.6 journey, 3 of 240 children (1.25%) lacked a wealth index and were dropped.

points.html: How to handle genuinely missing values depends on the missingness mechanism (§15.4.1).

If people with missing data differ systematically from the rest, dropping them distorts the sample in the same way as selection bias (§17.2.1: distortion that arises when remaining in the analysis depends on both exposure and outcome).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Missingness mechanisms are classified as (Sterne et al., 2009):

  • Missing completely at random (MCAR): the probability of being missing is unrelated to any values, observed or unobserved.
  • Missing at random (MAR): the probability of being missing depends only on observed variables; within groups defined by those variables, it is unrelated to the missing values themselves.
  • Missing not at random (MNAR): the probability of being missing depends on the unobserved value itself, even after allowing for the observed variables.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: “Random” is technical here. MAR does not mean haphazard; it means “explainable by what we did observe”. The mechanism cannot be proved from the data: “it is not possible to distinguish between missing at random and missing not at random using observed data” (Sterne et al., 2009). You argue for a mechanism from knowledge of how the data were collected.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
• MCAR: a haemoglobin sample is lost because a centrifuge failed, regardless of the woman.
  • MAR: women with no schooling are more likely to leave the wealth items blank; within each education group, whether the items are blank is unrelated to the household’s actual wealth.
  • MNAR: the richest households refuse the income question because their income is high.

points.html: MCAR: unrelated to anything. MAR: explained by observed variables. MNAR: depends on the missing value itself.
MAR versus MNAR cannot be tested from the observed data (Sterne et al., 2009); argue from how the data were collected.
Standard GEE needs MCAR (recall §15.2.5).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The main approaches are complete-case analysis (listwise deletion: analyse only records with no missing values), single imputation (fill each gap with one value, such as the mean), and multiple imputation (§15.4.3).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Complete-case analysis always loses precision. Whether it also loses validity depends on the mechanism and on the analysis. It is unbiased under MCAR. “When it is plausible that data are missing at random, but not completely at random, analyses based on complete cases may be biased” (Sterne et al., 2009). In a regression, however, “missing data in predictor variables also do not cause bias in analyses of complete cases if the reasons for the missing data are unrelated to the outcome” (Sterne et al., 2009). So complete cases are sometimes fine; decide case by case.

Mean imputation keeps the sample size but pretends to know what it does not. Every filled-in value sits at the centre, so the variable’s variance shrinks (recall §3.6), its correlations with other variables are diluted, and the SE is too small because the imputed values are treated as data. If missingness is related to the value, the mean is also biased.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Take the CBHI wealth index (true mean −0.196) and delete 72 of the 500 values (14.4%) by a MAR mechanism: 25% of households with no maternal education lose their value, against 10.7% with primary and 7.1% with secondary education, and members are less often missing than non-members. (The deletion is simulated by computer, so the truth is known.)

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Complete-case mean of the 428 remaining values = −0.080 (SE 0.086). It is too high by 0.116, because the poorer, less-educated households are the ones missing.
  2. Mean imputation fills the 72 gaps with −0.080. The mean stays at −0.080 (still biased); the SD falls from 1.77 in the complete cases to 1.64; the naive SE becomes 1.64/√500 = 0.073, smaller than the complete-case SE, although no information was added.

points.html: Complete cases: unbiased under MCAR; can be biased under MAR; in regression, unbiased if missingness in predictors is unrelated to the outcome (Sterne et al., 2009). Always loses precision.
Mean imputation shrinks variance, distorts associations and gives falsely small SEs. Avoid it for inference.
Under MNAR no method using only the observed data is guaranteed to work; use sensitivity analysis (§15.4.3).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Multiple imputation (MI) fills each missing value m times with values drawn from their predictive distribution given the observed data, analyses each of the m completed datasets with the planned analysis, and combines the m results by Rubin’s rules:

  • pooled estimate Q̄ = the mean of the m estimates;
  • within-imputation variance Ū = the mean of the m squared SEs;
  • between-imputation variance B = the variance of the m estimates;
  • total variance T = Ū + (1 + 1/m) × B, and SE = √T (van Buuren, Flexible Imputation of Missing Data, §2.3).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A missing value is not known, but it is not unknown either: education, distance and membership narrow down what a household’s wealth could be. MI draws a plausible value from that narrowed range, with deliberate randomness, so the same gap is filled differently in each completed dataset. The analysis is repeated in each; if the m answers agree, the missing values matter little, and if they disagree, B is large. Rubin’s rules add that disagreement to the ordinary sampling variance, so “standard errors … take account of the variability in results between the imputed datasets, reflecting the uncertainty associated with the missing values” (Sterne et al., 2009). The (1 + 1/m) term allows for using a finite number of imputations.

MI is not “guessing the right value”. It works by representing the spread of plausible values honestly.

The imputation model is not the analysis model. The imputation model should include the analysis variables (including the outcome) and auxiliary variables that predict the missing values or their missingness, even if they play no part in the analysis. Standard MI is justified under MAR, and only if the variables that explain the missingness are in the imputation model. It cannot repair MNAR: “if individuals are more likely to miss appointments because they are depressed on the day of the appointment, then it may be impossible to make the missing at random assumption plausible, even if a large number of variables is included in the imputation model” (Sterne et al., 2009).

Sensitivity analysis. When MNAR is plausible, repeat the analysis under less convenient assumptions (for example, imputed incomes shifted upwards by a stated amount) and report whether the conclusion survives.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Continue the §15.4.2 example: 72 wealth values deleted under MAR. Impute m = 20 times, using maternal education, distance, membership and household size, and estimate the mean wealth index in each completed dataset.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. The 20 estimates range from −0.235 to −0.126 (Figure 15.6). Q̄ = their mean = −0.176.
  2. Ū = 0.00625 (mean of the 20 squared SEs); B = 0.000567 (variance of the 20 estimates).
  3. T = 0.00625 + (1 + 1/20) × 0.000567 = 0.00625 + 0.000596 = 0.00685. SE = √0.00685 = 0.083.
  4. 95% CI: −0.339 to −0.013. The true mean, −0.196, lies inside; the complete-case mean, −0.080, is well away from it.
  5. The fraction of missing information is about 0.09: about 9% of the information about the mean was lost to the missing values, less than the 14.4% of values missing, because the observed variables in the imputation model recover part of it.

blocks.alt: Twenty completed-dataset estimates and their Rubin’s-rules combination
blocks.caption: Figure 15.6. Mean wealth index estimated in each of 20 imputed datasets (points, 95% CIs). The orange line is the pooled estimate, exactly the mean of the 20 points (−0.176); the shaded band is its pooled 95% CI from Rubin’s rules. Dashed: true mean before deletion (−0.196). Dotted: complete-case mean (−0.080).

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(mice)
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
cb$maternal_education <- factor(cb$maternal_education,
  levels = c("none", "primary", "secondary+"))
# the truth, before we delete anything
mean(cb$wealth_index)
# delete wealth: MAR, more often if no education
set.seed(15)
p_miss <- plogis(-2.2 + 1.5 * (cb$maternal_education == "none") -
                   0.8 * cb$cbhi_member)
cb$wealth_obs <- ifelse(runif(500) < p_miss, NA, cb$wealth_index)
# complete-case mean
sum(is.na(cb$wealth_obs)); mean(cb$wealth_obs, na.rm = TRUE)
imp <- mice(cb[, c("wealth_obs", "maternal_education", "distance_km",
                   "cbhi_member", "household_size")],
            m = 20, method = "pmm", seed = 15, printFlag = FALSE)
# analysis model: the mean
fits <- with(imp, lm(wealth_obs ~ 1))
round(summary(pool(fits), conf.int = TRUE)[,
  c("estimate", "std.error", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")], 3)
round(pool(fits)$pooled[, c("ubar", "b", "t", "fmi")], 5)
[1] -0.19578
[1] 72
[1] -0.08025701
  estimate std.error  2.5 % 97.5 %
1   -0.176     0.083 -0.339 -0.013
     ubar       b       t     fmi
1 0.00625 0.00057 0.00685 0.09168

The first three lines are the truth (−0.196), the number deleted (72) and the biased complete-case mean (−0.080). mice creates 20 completed datasets by predictive mean matching (pmm: each gap is filled with an observed wealth value from a household whose predicted wealth is close). with runs the analysis in each and pool applies Rubin’s rules: estimate −0.176, SE 0.083. The last line shows Ū, B, T and the fraction of missing information, as in the Worked Calculation.

points.html: MI: m completed datasets → m analyses → Rubin’s rules. Q̄ = mean; T = Ū + (1 + 1/m)B.
Include the outcome and auxiliary variables in the imputation model; it need not match the analysis model.
Valid under MAR with an adequate imputation model; not a remedy for MNAR (Sterne et al., 2009). Pair it with a sensitivity analysis.
Report the amount of missing data, the mechanism assumed, the imputation model, m, and the complete-case result alongside the MI result.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.7

questions.prompt: 15% of income values are missing, mostly among the wealthiest respondents, who are reluctant to disclose income. Will standard MAR-based multiple imputation remove the bias? What should the analyst do?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. If high income itself causes non-response, the data are MNAR: even within groups defined by the observed variables, the missing incomes are higher than the observed ones. Standard MI assumes MAR and would impute values that are too low. The analyst should include every variable that predicts income or its missingness (to make MAR as plausible as possible), then run a sensitivity analysis that imputes incomes shifted upwards by stated amounts and report whether the conclusion changes.

questions.prompt: Five imputed datasets give estimates 2.0, 2.4, 2.2, 1.8 and 2.1 for a regression coefficient, each with SE 0.30. Apply Rubin’s rules to find the pooled estimate and its SE.
questions.answer:
1. Q̄ = (2.0 + 2.4 + 2.2 + 1.8 + 2.1) ÷ 5 = 10.5 ÷ 5 = 2.10.
  2. Ū = 0.30² = 0.09 (all five SEs equal).
  3. Deviations from 2.10: −0.1, 0.3, 0.1, −0.3, 0.0; squares sum to 0.20. B = 0.20 ÷ (5 − 1) = 0.05.
  4. T = 0.09 + (1 + 1/5) × 0.05 = 0.09 + 0.06 = 0.15. SE = √0.15 = 0.387, compared with 0.30 in any single completed dataset.

questions.prompt: Why might the imputation model for missing income include “survey enumerator ID”, a variable that will never appear in the analysis model?
questions.answer: The imputation model’s job is to make MAR plausible and to predict the missing values well. Non-response often depends on who asked the question, so enumerator ID can explain the missingness; including it moves the mechanism towards MAR given the observed data. It has no role in the research question, so it stays out of the analysis model. The two models serve different purposes (Sterne et al., 2009).
